About the author

Odile Hartwell writes novels about families, weather and the places people refuse to leave.

She grew up on a fruit farm, studied botany before she studied literature, and now lives in a small coastal town with a large number of books and a small, opinionated cat.

Her novels have been translated into eleven languages. She teaches a summer workshop on revision and writes a monthly letter about reading.

pages.title: The Salt Orchard
pages.content:
Agathe has walked the rows of her orchard every morning for fifty years. Now the sea is coming, a little closer every winter, and her family cannot agree on whether to fight it or let the orchard go.

A novel to read slowly, by a window, with an apple.

pages.title: About
pages.content:
Odile Hartwell grew up on a fruit farm on a windy coast, where she learned to prune trees before she learned to read. She studied botany, then literature, then spent ten years working in bookshops before her first book was published.

She is the author of two novels, a book of essays and a collection of stories, translated into eleven languages.

Writing

She writes in the mornings, by hand first, at a table by a window that looks onto a small and disorderly garden. Afternoons are for reading, walking and answering letters, which she does very slowly but always does.

I write about people who stay. It is the bravest thing I know.

From an interview

Teaching

Each summer she teaches a week-long workshop on revision for writers who have finished a first draft and do not know what to do next. Details are announced in the monthly letter.

posts.title: The Salt Orchard Is Out Today
posts.excerpt: Seven years, four drafts and one orchard that refused to stay fictional. The new novel is in bookshops from this morning.
posts.content:
This morning, The Salt Orchard arrived in bookshops. I walked to the little shop on Quay Street before it opened, just to see it in the window, and found the owner already arranging copies into a small, unsteady tower.

The novel follows three generations of a family who farm apples on a strip of coast where the sea keeps creeping inland. It began as a short story in 2019 and grew, slowly and stubbornly, into the longest thing I have ever written.

Where to find it

  • In hardback from your local independent bookshop
  • As an audiobook, read beautifully by an actor whose voice I now hear in my sleep
  • In libraries from November: please ask for it, librarians do listen

Thank you to everyone who read early drafts, sent encouraging letters and asked, kindly and repeatedly, whether it was finished yet. It is. I hope it keeps you up a little past your bedtime.

posts.title: On Keeping a Commonplace Book
posts.excerpt: A notebook for other people's sentences: why I have kept one for twenty years, and how to start your own.
posts.content:
For twenty years I have kept a commonplace book: a notebook where I copy out sentences that stop me in my tracks. Not my own sentences, but other people's, from novels, letters, recipes, overheard conversations and the backs of seed packets.

The habit is centuries old. Readers once kept these books as a way of building a private library of thought, and I have come to think of mine as a conversation with every writer I have loved.

How to begin

  1. Choose a notebook you are not afraid to ruin.
  2. Copy by hand. The slowness is the point.
  3. Write where the sentence came from, and the date.
  4. Re-read it in winter, when you need it most.

Copying a sentence by hand teaches you how it is built: where it breathes, where it turns. Half of what I know about rhythm I learned from the ink on my own fingers.

comments.author: Juno
comments.content: I started one after your reading in the spring. It is already my favourite object in the house.

posts.title: Notes on Revision: The Fourth Draft
posts.excerpt: The first draft is a conversation with yourself. The fourth is a conversation with the reader. What changed, and what I cut.
posts.content:
People often ask how many drafts a novel takes. The honest answer is: as many as it takes to stop lying. The Salt Orchard needed four.

The first draft was three hundred pages of me finding out what the story was about. The second cut a whole point of view. The third moved the ending to the middle. The fourth, the one you can now read, was mostly about trust: trusting the reader to notice what I no longer needed to say.

What I cut

  • A seventy-page flashback to 1952
  • A talking dog (I am not sorry)
  • Every sentence beginning with 'Suddenly'
  • The prologue, twice
  • Two weddings and one funeral
  • Eleven thousand words about apple varieties

Revision is not fixing what is broken. It is finding out what the book has been trying to be all along.

If you are in the middle of your own revision, take heart. The pages you cut are not wasted. They are the scaffolding the finished book stood on while it was being built.

posts.title: A Signing Tour Diary, by Train
posts.excerpt: Nine cities, eleven bookshops, one lost umbrella. Notes scribbled between stations on the first leg of the tour.
posts.content:
I am writing this on the 16:42, somewhere between the river towns and the hills, with a cold coffee and a tote bag full of pens that may or may not work.

The thing nobody tells you about touring is how much listening you do. I arrive with a reading prepared, but the best part of every evening is the questions, and the stories readers tell me about their own families and their own orchards.

Next week: the coast, a literary festival in a marquee, and, I am told, a lighthouse. Fittingly.

comments.author: Ada
comments.content: The stairs at The Lantern were the best seats in the house. Thank you for staying so late.

posts.title: An Excerpt: The First Frost
posts.excerpt: The opening pages of The Salt Orchard, in which a grandmother walks the rows before dawn and the sea comes a little closer.
posts.content:
The first frost came in the night, the way it always did, without asking. By morning the orchard had turned to glass, and Agathe walked the rows with a lantern though the sky was already greying, because she had walked them with a lantern for fifty years and saw no reason to stop now.

She counted the trees as she went. Not the apples, which would come in their own time, but the trees themselves, as if one might have slipped away to the sea while she slept. Four hundred and twelve. The same as yesterday. The same, very nearly, as the year her husband planted the last of them.

At the end of the twelfth row the ground changed. It was soft there, and smelled of salt, and the grass had a grey edge to it that had not been there in spring. Agathe stood a long time looking at it, the lantern hissing in her hand.

Behind her, the farmhouse windows were lighting one by one: her son, who would want to talk about selling; her granddaughter, who would want to talk about anything else. Agathe turned her back on the sea and went in to make the porridge. There would be time enough for the twelfth row.

From The Salt Orchard, chapter one.

comments.author: Pell
comments.content: That last line. I had to put the book down and look out of the window for a while.

posts.title: Five Novels for a Long Winter
posts.excerpt: Thick books, slow books, books for the dark evenings. A reading list for the months when the lamp goes on at four.
posts.content:
Every year, around the time the clocks change, I start building a winter pile. These are the books I save for the dark months, when there is nothing better than a long story and a lamp.

This year's pile

  1. The Glass Valley: a family saga set in a glassblowing town, four hundred pages of heat and light.
  2. Ninety Letters to the Lighthouse: an epistolary novel that will make you want to write to someone.
  3. The Cartographer's Apprentice: maps, mountains and a mystery that unfolds very, very slowly.
  4. Small Hours: a quiet, funny novel about a night-shift baker. Read it with toast.
  5. A Year of Rivers: not a novel, strictly, but a book of seasons to dip into all winter.

How I read in winter

One long book at a time, one chapter a night, and never on a screen after nine. I keep a pencil in every book for underlining and for writing the date I finished it on the last page.

What is on your winter pile? Tell me in the comments: I am always looking for the next one.

comments.author: Mina
comments.content: Small Hours is my favourite book of the decade. Toast is essential.

comments.author: Rafe
comments.content: Adding The Glass Valley to my list. I need something long for January.

posts.title: Reading Notes: The Quiet Shelf
posts.excerpt: On books that do not shout: short novels, small presses and the pleasure of a story that trusts you to lean in.
posts.content:
In my study there is one shelf I call the quiet shelf. It holds the books that never made a splash: short novels from small presses, collections of poems with plain covers, memoirs about gardens and grief and the weather.

They are the books I press into friends' hands most often, precisely because nobody else will. A quiet book asks you to lean in. It does not explain itself. It trusts you.

The quietest books are often the ones that keep talking long after you close them.

Three from the shelf

  • The Ferryman's Almanac, a slim novel told in tide tables and weather notes.
  • Salt and Ash, poems about a fishing village, read aloud in one sitting.
  • A Patient Garden, a year in a walled garden, month by month.

If you run a small press or a bookshop with a quiet shelf of your own, I would love to hear what is on it.

posts.title: Ten Questions About The Salt Orchard
posts.excerpt: Readers sent questions; I tried to answer them honestly. On orchards, endings, grandmothers and the sea.
posts.content:
Before publication I asked readers of this letter what they wanted to know about the new novel. Hundreds of you wrote in. Here are ten of my favourite questions, with the most honest answers I could manage.

Is the orchard real?

Not exactly. It is three orchards I know, stitched together and moved closer to the sea than any sensible farmer would plant.

Who is Agathe based on?

Nobody and everybody. She has my grandmother's hands and my own stubbornness, and a temper all her own.

Why did the ending change?

Because the first ending was the one I wanted, and the final ending is the one the book needed.

What are you writing next?

Something shorter, set in a lighthouse, with far fewer apples.

Thank you for every question, including the one about whether I have ever eaten a salted apple. (Yes. Do not.)

The rest of the questions and answers will go out in next month's letter, along with a recipe for the apple cake from chapter nine.

comments.author: Odile Hartwell
comments.content: Thank you all for such generous questions. More answers in the next letter!
